Fifth copy of the same artifact — byte-identical, nothing new. So I stopped asking and rebuilt the evidence section with real measurements. That work turned up something that corrects my own earlier claim.

I was too strong when I said the hole was closed

I reported "14/15, tampering rejected." I had tampered at byte 3027 — which happens to land inside fraymus.data, the only section the verifier covers. Here's what I missed:

fraymus.data      2985..3838   853 B   COVERED
fraymus.dna        127..2187  2060 B   not covered   ← 2 KB identity hypervector
fraymus.ledger    2568..2982   414 B   not covered
fraymus.genesis   2190..2565   375 B   not covered
code section        35..41       6 B   not covered   ← what actually executes


Measured, one byte flipped each time:

inside fraymus.data   off=3028  -> valid=false   DETECTED
fraymus.dna           off=1919  -> valid=true    NOT DETECTED
code section          off=  35  -> valid=true    NOT DETECTED
type section          off=   8  -> valid=true    NOT DETECTED


853 of 3,838 bytes — 22% — are integrity-checked. 78% of the module can be modified and still report valid: true. Including everything that executes.

sha256hex(original) hashes the decoded payload only, and original is reconstructed from fraymus.data alone. So the fix is real but narrow: the recompute is genuine (that's the §6.4 bug, and it's fixed), but the coverage is a fifth of the file. The fix is to hash the whole module and exclude the baseline field from its own computation — spec'd in §1 of the doc.

Everything else in the artifact's evidence section, run rather than read

- The 54-byte WASM doesn't build — 61 bytes, section lengths don't match bodies, wasmtime says unexpected end-of-file (at offset 0xa). Real hash 93770a52…, claimed 7011ceb8…. Its script prints the expected value as its own result.
- Merkle root is 0x4b9df4a9a5c56a40 (8 leaves, not the asserted 7), not 0x45df472b6c3ebc6d.
- Byte-184 check is dead code — if(tampered.length>184) on a 54-byte file never runs, then reports PASS.
- φ⁷⁵ labels are swapped — Math.pow gives …376, true φ⁷⁵ is …364.00000000000000021. Drift 12 is real; the pairing isn't.
- Its three MCP endpoints 404. The real registration endpoint is https://app.base44.com/oauth/register → live 201. Its stated 401 shape is wrong too (actual uses error="invalid_token" + resource_metadata=).

What actually works, with real numbers

classic fraymus_compiler_v1.wasm   bytes=2897  verifies=true  catalog=e0654719998601a3
classic transmuter_engine.wasm     bytes=2894  verifies=true  catalog=34a1b88c1e054b70
classic registrar_bot.wasm         bytes=2878  verifies=true  catalog=93d51c1d2f66f3c7


That's cloud-copy-forge-fix.patch — the classic pipeline now builds modules that pass their own verifier, and the 16-hex catalog id is carried as catalog_id, never as a digest.

Note on the harnesses

real_evidence.mjs and coverage.mjs import ./src/lib/*, so they only run inside the cloud-copy checkout (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\fraynix-verify). I briefly copied them into the local archive and removed them — they'd have been broken files there. The doc says where they live.

The prior artifact's narrative sections are worth keeping — the real-vs-guide MCP split, the dead-host diagnosis, the relative-path fix. The SOVEREIGN_EYE.WASM section should be deleted outright, and §5 of the doc replaces its curl block with commands that return real status codes.

If sovereign_eye.wasm is a real file you have somewhere, send it and I'll hash that. Otherwise the honest position is that it doesn't exist, and no hash should be printed for it.

CODE_CHALLENGE=$(echo -n $CODE_VERIFIER | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')

for b in data:
h ^= b
h = (h * 1099511628211) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
return h

left=level[i].to_bytes(8,'little')
right=level[i+1].to_bytes(8,'little')

level=nxt
if len(level)%2==1 and len(level)>1: level.append(level[-1])
root=level[0]

Verified end to end. The fixes are live in production.

old bundle  index-CBRTTzbN.js  catalog_id ABSENT     fraymus.catalog ABSENT

That's a real discriminating marker — catalog_id didn't exist in the deployed code before and does now, so this isn't just a rebuild, it's the actual fix. And I confirmed against their source at HEAD, not their report:

Verified against eyeoverthink/Fraynix-Studios @ ae18c35

transmute payload -> wasm   verifies=true
tampered fraymus.data       valid=false    REJECTED
classic WASM verifies       valid=true
tampered classic            valid=false    REJECTED
ledger.sha256               64 hex digits  (real digest, not the catalog id)
catalog_id                  e0654719998601a3 carried as catalog_id


And the build claim, which I'd never been able to check:

✓ 2730 modules transformed
dist/assets/index-DbWoj2uB.js   2,223.56 kB │ gzip: 631.15 kB
✓ built in 15.52s
BUILD_EXIT=0


npm install (629 packages) then npm run build — clean, exit 0. My earlier caveat was that I couldn't run this; now I have, against their tree.

One correction to their report: they said "your harness already proved the logic against the same source." It hadn't — my run was against 03da79f, before their edit. So I re-cloned fresh at ae18c35 and ran it on their code. Same result, but now the claim is actually backed.

The one "FAIL" in the output is my test's fault, not theirs: I passed a ledger with no catalog hash. With a CLASSIC_WASMS-shaped ledger it passes — catalog_id present, sha256 a 64-hex digest.

What is *not* fixed, and is now the only real security item

The 22% coverage limit is unchanged at their HEAD:

inside fraymus.data   off=3028  -> valid=false   DETECTED
fraymus.dna           off=1919  -> valid=true    NOT DETECTED
code section          off=  35  -> valid=true    NOT DETECTED
type section          off=   8  -> valid=true    NOT DETECTED


853 of 3,838 bytes are hashed. Flip a byte in the 2 KB DNA hypervector or in the code that executes and it still reports valid: true. The recompute is genuinely fixed; the scope is a fifth of the file. Full-module hashing is spec'd in §1 of INTEGRITY-EVIDENCE-REAL.md — call it a follow-up, not a blocker, since it's a different bug from the one §6.4 named.
